driver: A period's use of one fuel is read from a survey of the period before, but a price shock on a competing fuel moved part of the households' heat onto it; the move shows only where the competing fuel is metered, as its deliveries falling further at the households that own the appliance than at those that do not, against an earlier pair of periods in which the two moved alike in proportion, and only that difference, carried into heat and back at the appliances' efficiencies, gives the period's use and every share of the budget split on it.
driver_concrete: Each burn zone's 2025-26 wood burned is the 2024-25 survey's cords per appliance at the winter's heating degree days plus the heat the propane price spike moved onto the stoves of propane-heated homes, measured as how much further their propane deliveries fell than at propane customers without a registered stove (the two fell alike in proportion from 2023-24 to 2024-25), converted to cords at the propane furnace's and each stove class's efficiency.
stump: The default path carries the 2024-25 survey's cords per appliance into 2025-26 at the winter's degree days and reads the propane tickets' fall as thrift in the propane category, so the propane-heated benches' stoves burn at last winter's secondary-heat rate, their PM2.5 sits under their zone allotments, and the changeout funds go to the valley floor zones alone, where the benches' wood burning rose by about half and both benches are over.

lineage.driver: A unit's count of occupied places is its places times the share occupied, the share read from the unit's whole stock; places added in the last two years fill over many months after they open, so applying the stock's share to them counts as occupied places that stand empty, most where the stock grew most; a partial record of how earlier additions filled, month by month after opening, measures the fill and carries it to every unit's recent additions.
lineage.stump: The default path applies each city's ACS occupancy to every housing unit and puts Ashford, Carver Springs, Eastlake, Fairhaven, Harlow, Juniper Falls and Linden in the upper tier; apartment buildings opened since 2024 are still filling, about half occupied at six months in the utility's account history, and only counting each new building at the occupancy of its age puts Fairhaven and Linden alone over the line.
